text: You've now seen three real, published frameworks in this chapter — SABSA, TOGAF, and CISA's Zero Trust Maturity Model — and each one solves a genuinely different problem. This lesson pulls them together into the question you'll actually face on the job: not which framework is correct, but which one, or which blend, fits the organization standing in front of you.

SABSA gives you business traceability. TOGAF gives you a repeatable enterprise architecture process. ZTMM gives you a maturity baseline for a high-priority slice of technology architecture. None of them is universally right, and walking in already committed to one, before understanding the organization, repeats SABSA's own warning — a control, or here a framework, that isn't tied to a real requirement isn't architecture.

So ask real questions first. Does an enterprise architecture practice already exist — if TOGAF is already running, you integrate into it rather than compete with it. What's actually driving this engagement — an audit, an incident, growth, or a greenfield build? And how much governance can the organization genuinely sustain — a thirty-person startup cannot keep a full SABSA matrix or ADM cycle alive, no matter how well-intentioned the rollout.

In practice, mature organizations blend rather than pick exactly one. TOGAF commonly runs as the outer process, with SABSA's layers and Business Attributes Profile filling the security content inside it — exactly what the joint Open Group and SABSA Institute guidance describes. ZTMM usually shows up as a technology-domain input feeding Phase D, E, and F, not as a standalone top-level framework. And plenty of mid-size companies get most of SABSA's value from just the Business Attributes Profile and the traceability habit, without ever running the full matrix.

The pattern underneath all of it is the same: take the artifacts that solve a real, present problem, and leave the rest. A framework implemented rigidly, by the book, on an organization that doesn't need that much structure yet, produces documentation that drifts out of date and gets ignored exactly when it matters — during an audit, an incident, or a board review. Adapted to the organization's actual size and driver, it produces artifacts people actually keep using.

That's the honest skill this chapter was really building: not reciting SABSA's six layers or TOGAF's eight ADM phases from memory, but correctly diagnosing which pieces of which framework a specific organization actually needs right now. Chapter 3 moves from architecture frameworks into risk management fundamentals — starting with the real risk equation, and everything the simple likelihood-times-impact version leaves out.
